title: Easter, fifty days
tomorrow: does the Spirit come once, or again every year?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three days: Thursday, Friday, and a Saturday of spices and rest. Then the stone moves, and the counting starts over.

Here's an odd bit of math in the Church year. Lent is forty days. Jesus fasted forty days in the desert. The book of Acts says the risen Jesus showed himself to his friends "for forty days appearing to them." Forty, forty, forty. And yet the Easter season isn't forty. The Church keeps it for fifty. Why would the feast run longer than the fast?
screen: `FORTY, FORTY, FORTY.` → `THEN FIFTY?` → `THE FEAST OUTLASTS THE FAST.`

segments.voice: Start with Acts. The forty days of appearances end when Jesus is taken up. Then the disciples wait together, and "when the days of the Pentecost were accomplished, they were all together in one place." Pentecost was already a Jewish feast, the feast of weeks, counted out from Passover in the Torah: seven full weeks, then the next day, fifty days in all. So Easter doesn't end when the appearances do. It runs on until the Spirit comes. The Church's norms say the fifty days from Easter Sunday to Pentecost are celebrated in joy as one feast day, even as one great Sunday. That's the answer to the puzzle. The fast is forty; the feast is fifty. On the Church's own calendar, joy gets ten more days than penance. The trouble is that the candy runs out by Tuesday. Easter week feels like Easter; week four feels like any other week. So fifty days of joy needs something small and repeatable, one Easter joy a week: a long meal with people you love, a walk somewhere green, a visit to someone who can't get out. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the Alleluia, silent through all of Lent, comes back at the Easter Vigil, and through the fifty days it's sung again and again.
screen: `TAKEN UP AFTER FORTY DAYS.` · `PENTECOST: THE FEAST OF WEEKS.` · `ONE GREAT SUNDAY.` · `ONE EASTER JOY A WEEK.` · then, large: `FIFTY DAYS OF JOY.`

segments.voice: Count joys on your fingers, slowly: one thing from this week that was good, then another, up to five if they come. Don't rank them or explain them; just count, and stay a moment with each. If you pray, you can say Alleluia once for each finger.
Easter. Not one Sunday but fifty days, kept as one feast all the way to Pentecost.
Here's the line: fifty days of joy, ten more than the fast ever got. See you tomorrow.

chat.meaning: The Church keeps the fifty days from Easter to Pentecost as one feast. Easter joy is meant to be kept, a little each week.

Pentecost.meaning: the feast fifty days after Easter, when the Spirit comes

Passover.meaning: the Jewish feast remembering the exodus from Egypt

Alleluia.meaning: a song of praise, kept silent during Lent

Easter Vigil.meaning: the night liturgy that opens Easter in the dark
